paragraphs.text: Before you begin
Moses Afolabi • Illustrated study edition • 2026

Read the whole Bible passage before working through a chapter. Scripture quotations use the King James Version. Modern application scenes and illustrations are teaching examples. They do not describe documented events or verified personal testimonies.
Historical accounts are identified and accompanied by source links. Consider their particular setting as you reflect on the biblical passage.

Take time to read the explanation, study the visual summary, and complete the practice in your own notebook. Discuss difficult questions with a trusted pastor or mature believer. Return to the chapter after trying its suggested action.
The PDF contains still illustrations. The separate animated companion adds gentle motion and chapter prompts.

Chapter 1 Coming to the Father
Begin together. The word “our” invites us to carry another person’s need before the same Father.
Read Matthew 6:5–13, Hebrews 4:14–16, and Luke 11:5–13. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.
Begin with the One who hears you
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. — Matthew 6:9

Read this verse in the order Jesus gives it. The prayer begins with the One we address, then speaks of His name, kingdom and will before asking for daily bread. If you usually pray only after a problem becomes urgent, you can still come immediately. The first words of the prayer give you a place to stand while you name the problem. You are bringing it to the Father Jesus teaches you to trust.

The word our also changes how you pray. A family may need food, a student may need strength to face an examination, and a pastor may need wisdom for a hard conversation. Each has an immediate concern. The plural address invites the person praying to remember others who depend on the same Father. After naming your own need, consider who else faces its consequences. Ask for patience for yourself and a fair hearing for the person with whom you disagree. Ask for provision for your household and remember a neighbor who faces a similar shortage. The shared language of the prayer can change which people you notice after praying.

Which art in heaven places the Father above every earthly authority and every account of fatherhood we have known. Some readers have received patient care from a parent. Others associate the word father with absence or fear. Let Jesus teach you whom you are addressing. A short beginning may be enough: “Father, teach me from Your Word what it means to come to You.” Keep reading until you can name one thing the passage says about God.
The Father who sees in secret

But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. — Matthew 6:6

Matthew 6 opens with a warning about practicing righteousness to be seen. Jesus then gives examples involving giving, prayer, and fasting. In the prayer example, a person who wants the attention of the onlookers has already obtained the reward they sought. The person who shuts the door gives up that audience and speaks to the Father. Jesus’ instruction gives a practical way to expose the desire to impress. Try praying about something you would hesitate to admit in a public gathering. You may find that private prayer makes your words plainer and your requests more precise.
Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. — Matthew 6:8

If the Father already knows, why ask? Watch what Jesus does next. He gives His disciples words with which to ask. Knowledge and invitation belong together. The person praying does not have to supply facts that God has missed. Naming the need can help that person receive help, recognize dependence, and act with a clearer heart. A mother praying over a dispute at home can name the exact moment she lost her temper. She can ask for grace to apologize and decide how she will make time to listen.
Why believers can draw near

For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. — Hebrews 4:15–16

The word therefore matters. The invitation to come boldly follows the description of Jesus, our great High Priest. He understands weakness and remained without sin. Confidence begins with Him. A reader who has already spoken harshly can ask for mercy, and a reader still facing a difficult conversation can ask for grace to help before they speak. The passage welcomes both at the time they need help.

You can pray with reverence and speak plainly at the same time. State what you did, name what you need, and ask for the strength to take the next honest step. If you have hurt someone, consider what an appropriate correction would involve. If you are facing temptation, identify the decision where help is needed. Let the request become specific enough that you recognize the next faithful action when it becomes available.
Scriptural testimony · The father of a suffering child
And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. — Mark 9:24

Read Mark 9:14–29. The father came to Jesus after the disciples had been unable to help his child. When Jesus addressed him, he brought faith and struggle into the same sentence. His request concerns his child and also his own need for help. The story gives a reader language for the moment when they know enough to turn to Christ and still feel uncertain. A prayer can begin precisely there.

Compare the father’s request with Hebrews 4:16. Hebrews invites believers to draw near in their time of need. Mark shows someone naming that need in front of Jesus. Use the two texts together. Name the situation in which you need help, then name the weakness or fear that makes it hard for you to pray about it.
Historical testimony · George Müller prays about an orphan house

In his first published narrative, George Müller records how he prayed in late 1835 while considering an orphan house in Bristol. His November 28 entry describes asking God to take the idea from him if it was outside God’s will and examining his motives. On December 5, while reading Psalm 81:10, he began praying for particular needs, including premises, funds, and people suited to care for children. He records that he placed those requests before God without setting a date by which they had to be granted.

His account is instructive because it records the questions before the outcome. He considered whether to undertake the work, then made his requests specific. A reader praying over a new ministry or responsibility can follow a similar sequence. Ask why you want to do it, who would be affected, and what would be required to serve them well. A prayer for children who need care should lead the person praying to think about a safe place, suitable adults, and ongoing support.

Psalm 81 recalls God bringing Israel out of Egypt and calling His people to listen to Him. Müller records how one verse turned his attention toward asking plainly for provision. When reading his testimony, keep the psalm’s context in view and distinguish Müller’s particular request from the general invitation Jesus gives His disciples to pray. George Müller, A Narrative of Some of the Lord’s Dealings with George Müller, Part 1, entries for November 28 and December 5, 1835

Father’s invitation
Name the need honestly
Draw near through Christ
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Workbook practice · Pray and act on one real need

Read Matthew 6:9 and Hebrews 4:16 aloud once. Write the name of one person or concern you have avoided bringing to prayer. Describe the situation in one sentence a trusted friend could understand. Draw a line under the facts and put a question mark beside any assumption.
Now complete these requests in your own words.
1. Mercy. “Father, where I have failed in this matter, I ask You for mercy concerning ___.”
2. Grace. “I need Your help today when I have to ___.”
3. Care for another person. “Please help ___, who is also affected by ___.”
4. A step I can take. “Before the day ends, I can ___.”

At the end of the day, revisit what you wrote. Record what changed, what you learned, and what still needs prayer. If you discovered that an assumption was wrong, rewrite the request using the facts you now know. Over several days, notice how praying from Scripture affects what you ask and how you act afterward.

Prayer. Father, I come to You through Jesus Christ. You know my need before I speak. Give me mercy where I have failed and grace where I need strength. Show me the people whose burdens I have overlooked. Help me take the next faithful step in Your presence. Amen.
Chapter 2 Hallowed Be Thy Name
Let praise grow from attention to God’s character. Gratitude gives ordinary moments a language of worship.
Read Matthew 6:9, Psalm 103:1–14, and Exodus 34:5–7.

To hallow God’s name is to regard it as holy. In Scripture, God’s name identifies the One who acts and makes Himself known. In Exodus, the Lord proclaims His name to Moses and describes His mercy, patience, faithfulness, and justice. Israel has already broken covenant in the episode of the golden calf. This makes the revelation of His character more significant. He speaks about mercy where there has been real wrongdoing, and His mercy does not remove the seriousness of what happened.

Begin your worship with one such detail. In Psalm 103, David recalls the benefits of the Lord and then speaks of God’s compassion toward those who fear Him. Verse 14 gives a reason for that compassion. He remembers that we are dust. Let the movement of that sentence guide you. Name a weakness you usually hide. Then thank God for the compassion the psalm describes. When the words of Scripture are specific, your worship can become specific too.
Worship when the news is disappointing

A shopkeeper in Accra receives a message that an expected delivery has been delayed. People have already paid deposits. He knows that anger will tempt him to make a promise about the new delivery date before he has checked it. He reads Psalm 103:8 and gives thanks that God is patient. Then he asks for patience to call each customer honestly. The delivery has yet to arrive. His worship has already shaped how he treats the people waiting for it.

The phrase “Hallowed be thy name” also asks for something beyond your private moment. You are asking that God be honored. If you pray this before answering a frustrated customer or a family member, let it reach your tone and your willingness to admit what you know. A brief prayer can be followed by a slower, more truthful response.
Holiness in the presence of God
And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory. — Isaiah 6:3, KJV

Read Isaiah 6:1–8 in sequence. Isaiah hears the seraphim call the Lord holy. He then acknowledges the uncleanness of his lips and the lips of his people. A seraph brings a coal from the altar and declares his sin purged. Finally, when the Lord asks whom He will send, Isaiah offers himself. Worship, confession, cleansing, and service belong to the same encounter, and each changes how you read the next. Isaiah cannot offer himself with a clear understanding of the commission while ignoring what he has just seen about himself.

This helps when the words “Hallowed be thy name” feel abstract. Begin by naming what you see in the passage. Then allow God’s character to expose something specific in your own conduct. If you have used speech to injure someone, Isaiah’s reference to his lips gives you a place to begin. Ask for mercy, then consider a practical act of service that uses those same lips honestly. You might correct a false impression you helped create or defend someone whose contribution you ignored.
Mercy and justice in the same proclamation
And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, — Exodus 34:6, KJV

Continue into verse 7. The Lord declares that He forgives iniquity, transgression, and sin, and that He takes guilt seriously. Moses is hearing these words after Israel’s worship of the golden calf. Read Exodus 32:1–8 and 34:8–9 to see why both parts matter. The people have a history they cannot excuse, and Moses responds by bowing, worshiping, and asking the Lord to pardon them and go with them.

If you are responsible for a group, pray this passage before responding to a failure. Decide which facts need to be established, who has been affected, and which process can address the wrong. Then ask God for the patience to hear people and the courage to speak truthfully. You can seek accountability and pray for a person’s good in the same situation. God’s patience gives you reason to proceed carefully even when others want an immediate verdict.
Historical testimony · A hymn shaped by what Scripture says

Reginald Heber wrote the text of the hymn commonly known as Holy, Holy, Holy for Trinity Sunday. Hymnary identifies the hymn’s links with Isaiah 6 and with Revelation’s worship scenes. The Book of Common Prayer assigned Revelation 4 for that occasion. Heber’s work gives a historical example of a writer taking the language and images of Scripture into the public worship of a congregation.
Read Revelation 4:8–11 and look for what the worshipers give as a reason for honoring

God. Creation belongs to His pleasure and purpose. A congregation singing about holiness can remember that the world it prays for is the world God made. You can use the same principle in private prayer. Let a specific biblical reason lead to a specific sentence of praise. Hymnary.org, Holy, Holy, Holy! Lord God Almighty!
Carry worship into a difficult conversation

A parent hears that a child has been blamed for damaging a classroom book. The first impulse may be to defend the child before learning what happened. Begin with the character God declares in Exodus 34:6. His patience gives you reason to hear the teacher carefully. His truth calls you to ask the child an open question and allow time for an honest answer. His mercy guides the response if the child admits responsibility. Each part of the passage directs a particular part of the conversation.

Prepare three questions. What has been observed? Who has been affected? What response would help address the harm? If responsibility is clear, discuss how the book can be replaced or repaired. If the facts remain uncertain, agree on how they will be checked. Keep the child's dignity in view while taking the teacher's concern seriously. Pray afterward about the moment when you most wanted to interrupt or accuse. Let the next conversation show the patience and truth you have praised in God.

See God’s character
Honor His name in prayer
Reflect His character in conduct
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
A three-day practice
1. Choose one statement about God from Exodus 34:6–7 or Psalm 103.
2. Write what the passage says in your own words and name one situation that calls for that truth.
3. Turn the truth into a sentence of praise. Follow it with one request about your own conduct.
4. Review that request in the evening. Where did you have an opportunity to honor the name you prayed about?

On the first day read Exodus 34:6–9 and write one sentence of praise. On the second, read Isaiah 6:1–8 and ask what part of your speech needs change. On the third, read Revelation 4:8–11 and give thanks for one part of creation you usually overlook. At the close of the third day, write down one sentence you want to carry into next week.

Prayer. Father, Your name is holy. You are merciful, patient, and true. Teach me to remember Your character when my mind is occupied with what has gone wrong. Let my words and decisions honor You today. Amen.
Chapter 3 Thy Kingdom Come
Prayer for God’s kingdom can lead into willing service. Ask whose need you can help meet today.
Read Matthew 6:10, Matthew 5:3–10, and Matthew 9:35–38.

A kingdom involves the rule of a king. Jesus teaches His disciples to ask for the coming of God’s kingdom. In Matthew, He announces the kingdom and demonstrates His authority as He teaches, heals, and shows compassion. His disciples are also taught to look ahead to the fulfillment of God’s purposes. This petition gives them words for both the present need and the future hope. Pray for God’s rule to be seen where people are hurting, and long for the day when His purposes are fully accomplished.

At the end of Matthew 9, Jesus sees the crowds and has compassion on them. He tells the disciples to pray for workers for the harvest. Notice who sees the need, who is asked to pray, and who is asked to send the workers. If a need frustrates you, practice looking at the people the way Jesus does in this passage. You may be able to name a need more clearly after you have listened to someone describe it.
Pray over one place you know

In Nairobi, two people in a congregation notice that newcomers rarely return after their first visit. One assumption is that the newcomers are uninterested. A conversation reveals that several felt uncertain about where to go and how to get involved. The two believers begin praying that people will be welcomed and discipled. They also ask the church how they can serve. Their first assignment is modest. They help greet newcomers, show them where to sit, and ask whether they would welcome a follow-up call.

Your prayer may concern a different place. Think of a street, home, workplace, school, or congregation. Choose a situation where a prayer for peace, justice, mercy, or reconciliation can be made specific. Ask God to raise up people who can serve faithfully. Then ask whether a practical part of the work belongs to you and approach it with the people already responsible for that place.
Hear the request in the order Jesus gives it
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. — Matthew 6:10, KJV

The two sentences belong together. Asking for God’s kingdom to come leads immediately into asking for His will to be done. It is possible to pray for a change in the world while holding one’s own decisions outside the request. Jesus gives you words that reach both places. When you pray about violence, injustice, or neglect, ask where you have responsibility and what faithful conduct is available to you.
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. — Matthew 6:33, KJV

Read Matthew 6:25–34 for the things Jesus is discussing. He names food, drink, and clothing. These are needs the Father knows, and Jesus directs His disciples to seek God’s kingdom and righteousness first. A person anxious about provision can hear this instruction alongside the request for daily bread. Pray for what is needed, then ask which choice remains faithful while you wait. A person under pressure to make a sale might refuse to make a claim they cannot verify. A leader worried about a short budget might state the shortfall plainly and ask for counsel.
Scriptural testimony · The twelve are sent
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest. — Matthew 9:38, KJV

Read from Matthew 9:35 into Matthew 10:8. Jesus teaches, preaches, heals, and looks on the crowds with compassion. Then He asks the disciples to pray for workers. In the next chapter He calls the twelve and sends them. Their commission has a specific audience and instructions. The sequence connects prayer with being sent while still leaving the Lord of the harvest in charge of where people serve.

There are two questions to bring into your own prayer. What need have you actually seen? What part of the response are you equipped and authorized to undertake? A volunteer may see that a person needs counseling and be able to listen and direct them to appropriate help. A congregation may see that a family needs food and have a pantry already serving that neighborhood. Praying for workers can make you more attentive to the people, roles, and provisions already available.
Historical testimony · Taking the gospel into the streets

The Salvation Army traces its beginning to the work of William and Catherine Booth in East London in 1865. The early movement became known as the Christian Mission. Its institutional history describes an approach that brought preaching directly to people and developed practical forms of care, including shelter and food. These efforts took place among people who could easily be overlooked by institutions centered elsewhere.

That account gives a limited, concrete illustration of the movement from attention to service. The people praying about East London had to learn what people there faced and decide how to respond in that setting. If you are praying for your own neighborhood, ask people already working there which need they repeatedly encounter and where help is hardest to find. Their answers may direct you toward a simpler and more useful contribution than the one you originally imagined. The Salvation Army, Our History
Make the prayer specific without making it narrow

Consider a fictional group in Ibadan praying for young people looking for work. Their first request is broad. Over two conversations, they learn that some applicants need internet access to complete forms and others are looking for help reading job descriptions. They pray for trustworthy opportunities and appropriate support. One member arranges three supervised sessions at a community space. Another asks local employers to explain what information applicants need. The group leaves room to learn from the people it hopes to serve.

A useful prayer names the people, the need, and the good being sought. A useful act of service can then be assessed by whether it addressed the need people actually described. At the end of your first effort, ask one person what was helpful and what remained difficult. Bring their answer back into prayer. The second prayer may name a different barrier from the first.

Workbook practice · Pray, listen, and return

Sketch three small circles labeled home , community , and beyond . Choose one real need for each circle. Pray for a person as well as a result. Underline one matter on which you can take a faithful step this week. Leave room to write down what you learn from the people involved.
1. Name one place and one group of people you regularly encounter there.
2. Write a first prayer for that group and identify any assumption in it.
3. Ask someone with firsthand knowledge what you have overlooked.
4. Pray again using what you have learned. Ask for people who can serve well.
5. Choose one action you can take this week and one question you will ask afterward.

Prayer. Father, let Your kingdom come. Give us compassion for people we have overlooked. Raise up workers who will serve faithfully. Show me where to pray, where to listen, and where to offer help in Jesus’ name. Amen.
Chapter 4 Thy Will Be Done
Bring the decision into the light of Scripture. Wise counsel and honest facts help shape a faithful response.
Read Matthew 6:10, Matthew 26:36–46, and Romans 12:1–2.

In Gethsemane, Jesus names what He desires and submits Himself to the Father. Matthew records His sorrow and His repeated prayer. The scene gives a believer language for an honest request in a hard circumstance. You can say what you desire, bring the weight of it to God again, and place your decision before Him. Some acts of obedience begin while the grief is still real.

Romans 12 connects discernment to the renewing of the mind. Paul is speaking to believers about offering their lives to God. A prayer for God’s will can therefore include a review of what is shaping your judgment. Are you reacting to pressure, following a familiar habit, or hearing wise counsel? Consider which part of your decision Scripture addresses clearly and which part requires information you have yet to gather.
Work through a decision with two good options

A believer in Chengdu is offered a promotion that requires evening hours. The additional income would help at home. The change would also affect an existing family commitment. The believer prays honestly about wanting the role, speaks with the family, and asks the employer to clarify how often late evenings are required. The next decision can be made with a clearer understanding of the burden and the opportunity.

For a decision of your own, write the truthful desire first. List any clear responsibilities. Name one unknown you can check and a person whose perspective you should hear. Then pray again with what you have learned. When you choose an action, identify the part that calls for patience or courage after you decide.
Hear Jesus pray before you choose your words
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. — Matthew 26:39, KJV

Read Matthew 26:36–46 slowly. The narrative names Jesus’ sorrow before it records this prayer. He goes farther, falls on His face, and speaks to the Father. The request has a particular object, the cup before Him, and a submission to the Father. These details give the passage its weight. Jesus is facing the suffering that leads to the cross. His prayer belongs to His unique saving mission and also shows His disciples how honestly He addresses the Father in anguish.

When you bring a painful decision to God, name the desire plainly. An adult caring for a parent may pray that a difficult arrangement can change. A person asked to admit an error may wish that the conversation could be avoided. Having named the desire, ask what obedience requires in that situation. The next action may be to seek appropriate help, tell a person the truth, or keep a responsibility while a better arrangement is being considered. Prayer creates room to bring both desire and obedience before the Father.

Jesus returns to prayer after finding the disciples asleep. Verse 44 says He prayed again, saying the same words. Read that alongside His earlier teaching about empty repetition in Matthew 6:7. Repeating an honest request in distress can be a way of continuing to seek God. The problem Jesus describes in Matthew 6 concerns the belief that a large quantity of speech will secure a hearing. In Gethsemane, He continues addressing His Father about the same grave matter.
A renewed mind in a real decision
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. — Romans 12:2, KJV

Read Romans 12:1–8. Paul begins with the mercies of God and calls believers to offer themselves to Him. He then speaks of humility, different gifts, and service within the body. Seeking God’s will therefore reaches how you think about yourself and how your decision affects others. A person who prays over a new responsibility can ask whether they are assessing their capacity honestly and whether they have listened to the people who will share the work.

Write down the reasons you favor an option. Include reasons you are reluctant to admit, such as wanting recognition or fearing disappointment. Then ask which reasons Scripture affirms, which require examination, and which depend on facts you still need to learn. This exercise can help you pray with greater honesty. The desire you started with may become clearer, or you may see an opportunity to serve that you had overlooked.
Historical testimony · Müller describes seeking direction

In a statement reproduced in Answers to Prayer , George Müller describes beginning the process of discernment by seeking willingness to follow God’s will. He says he seeks direction through Scripture, considers circumstances, prays, and reaches a deliberate judgment. His description brings together willingness, attention to God’s Word, and practical consideration of the matter at hand.

His testimony offers a useful set of questions for a reader facing a choice. Would you hear an answer that disappoints your preference? Have you considered what Scripture says about the conduct involved? Have you gathered the facts that a responsible person would need? These questions can become a preparation for prayer and for the conversation with people affected by the choice. George Müller, Answers to Prayer, introductory section on discerning God’s will

Workbook practice · Name the next faithful action

Choose a decision with a real deadline. Write the deadline, the people affected, and the information you still need. Read Matthew 26:39 and pray an honest sentence about what you want. Read Romans 12:2 and ask God to renew the part of your thinking that needs examination. Before the deadline, make the necessary inquiry and speak with someone wise who understands the situation. Record your decision and one responsibility it creates for the week ahead.

Prayer. Father, You know what I want and what I fear. Renew my mind by Your Word. Give me wisdom to seek the facts and humility to hear people who will be affected by my choice. Help me obey what You have made clear. Amen.
Chapter 5 Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread
Daily bread connects dependence with gratitude, responsible work, and attention to a neighbor’s hunger.
Give us this day our daily bread. — Matthew 6:11, KJV

The prayer moves from God’s kingdom to the needs of people who must eat today. Jesus gives those needs a place in the same prayer. “This day” focuses attention on what is needed now. “Us” reminds you to ask for more than your own household. A person who has enough food can pray this petition as honestly as a person whose cupboard is empty. Both depend on provision they cannot entirely control.
Scriptural testimony · Manna for the day

Then said the LORD unto Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no. — Exodus 16:4, KJV

Read Exodus 16:13–30. The ordinary instruction required Israel to gather what they needed. The sixth day had a different instruction so the people could rest on the seventh. Read both parts before applying the passage. Preparing for a responsibility and depending on God can belong to the same act of obedience. The people still went out to gather the food they received.

If you are praying about an empty week of work, name what is needed today. Identify a person you can ask about an opening, an expense you can discuss before it becomes overdue, or practical help your household can receive. If a neighbor faces the same difficulty, ask what help would be welcome before deciding what they need.

Practice. Write two columns in a notebook. Put one present need under “Ask” and a responsible step under “Gather.” Choose one person to remember when you pray “us.” Review the request tomorrow and record what information or help arrived.
Receive the gift and gather it faithfully
And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground. — Exodus 16:14, KJV

Read Exodus 16:14–21. Israel encounters something unfamiliar and asks what it is. Moses identifies it as the bread the Lord has given. The people then gather according to the instruction. Notice the care given to household size. The amount is connected to the people who must eat. A prayer for daily bread invites you to be specific about the people for whom you have responsibility. What does the household need today? Who is unable to gather for themselves? How can the person receiving help be treated with dignity?

The account also records people keeping some until morning against the ordinary instruction. The food spoils. Later the sixth-day instruction provides for the Sabbath. Read the exception alongside the ordinary rule. Dependence on God includes attending to what He has actually said. The same act can be appropriate in one circumstance and disobedient in another. In your own situation, learn what is required before deciding that an attractive example from someone else’s life settles the question.
Scriptural testimony · A church shares with people in need
Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea: — Acts 11:29, KJV

Read Acts 11:27–30. A coming famine is reported, and the disciples determine to send help. The text identifies ability as the measure of each contribution and records who carries the relief to the elders. A need beyond the local congregation becomes an organized response. The passage gives you a way to pray daily bread for people you may never meet. Ask what they need, learn who can receive and distribute help responsibly, and give according to your ability.

For a family in Enugu praying over school expenses, the need may include transport, meals, and books as well as the fee named first. Make a simple list before deciding what kind of help to request. Ask the school which costs fall due now and which can be arranged later. If someone offers assistance, agree what it will cover. Plain information can make a modest contribution useful.

Name today’s need
Receive and work responsibly
Share with a neighbor
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Give thanks while the request is still open
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. — Philippians 4:6, KJV

Paul includes thanksgiving in the act of making requests. You can thank God for help already received while asking about the need still ahead. Write down a person who gave advice, a task you were able to finish, or a meal shared with you. Then name the unresolved matter without pretending it has disappeared. This keeps prayer truthful about the whole day.

At the close of the week, review the requests in your notebook. Identify what provision arrived, which actions you took, and what still requires attention. If another person’s need became clearer, update the prayer. Daily bread is a request you can return to with fresh knowledge of the people involved.
Prayer. Father, give us what we need today. Guide our work and help us receive what You provide with gratitude. Give me eyes to see who around me needs a share in what I have. Amen.
Chapter 6 Forgive Us Our Debts
Name the wrong plainly. Prepare an apology that accepts responsibility and offers an appropriate repair.
And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our
debtors. — Matthew 6:12, KJV

The language of debt makes wrongdoing concrete. Something is owed. Luke 11:4 uses the language of sins in the corresponding petition. When you pray this sentence, give God an honest description of the wrongdoing. “I said I would include her, then made the decision without telling her” is more useful than “Please forgive anything
I might have done.” Specific words help you see a responsibility that vagueness can conceal.
Scriptural testimony · David asks for a clean heart
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and
renew a right spirit within me. — Psalm

The heading of Psalm 51 connects the psalm to Nathan’s visit after David’s sin involving Bathsheba. Read 2 Samuel 12:1–13 with Psalm 51:1–12. Nathan brings the wrongdoing into view. David’s prayer asks for cleansing and renewal. The two passages together resist a shallow confession that only wants the consequences to go away. God’s mercy gives the person confessing a reason to tell the truth and seek change.

For a concrete example, suppose you spread an allegation in a group message before confirming it. Confess that specific act to God. Then think about the people who heard it and the person the allegation affected. A correction shared with the original audience may be needed. The wording can be direct: “I passed on a claim I had not verified. Please disregard it.” Avoid passing the accusation around again under cover of an apology.

Practice. Write what happened, what you were responsible for, and one appropriate repair. If a direct approach could put someone at risk or disregard a boundary, seek wise counsel about making a responsible correction.
Read confession in the light
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just
to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from
all unrighteousness. — 1 John 1:9, KJV

Read 1 John 1:5–10. John begins with God as light and then describes fellowship, truth, cleansing, and confession. The person confessing brings conduct into agreement with the truth. If you promised to include someone and deliberately left them out, use words that acknowledge the choice. Explain the action before describing the pressure you were under. Pressure may help you understand where to change, while the action still needs to be confessed.

The verse names God’s faithfulness and justice. A person who feels deeply ashamed can return to those words. When you ask forgiveness, you rely on the character of the One receiving the confession. Let that confidence help you take responsibility. If you need to correct an account or replace something you damaged, decide how to approach the person affected and carry out the repair you can reasonably make.
Scriptural testimony · The tax collector’s prayer
And the publican, standing afar off, would
not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven,
but smote upon his breast, saying, God be
merciful to me a sinner. — Luke 18:13, KJV

Read Luke 18:9–14. Jesus identifies the audience’s problem before telling the parable. Some trusted in their own righteousness and despised others. The Pharisee’s prayer names his practices while comparing himself favorably with other people. The tax collector asks for mercy. Jesus’ explanation directs the hearer toward humility. If confession becomes a recital of how much worse another person behaved, this parable gives you a place to stop and begin again.

Try writing a confession that contains no comparison. State the wrong, ask for mercy, and name one step toward a faithful response. Then ask whether you have made the person harmed responsible for reassuring you. An apology can become difficult for the listener when it is followed by an immediate demand to say that everything is well. Give the person room to respond and allow trust to take the time it needs.
Visual summary
Confess the specific wrong
Receive God’s forgiveness
Make an appropriate repair
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Work through a truthful correction

Imagine a fictional fellowship treasurer who records a payment under the wrong member’s name and lets the error stand because correcting it will be embarrassing. The next meeting begins with praise for the member who appears to have given. The treasurer can confess the concealment to God, confirm the original receipt, and ask the appropriate leader to correct the record. The correction should reach the people who relied on the mistaken information.
Write three drafts for an error of your own. The first names the facts privately before

God. The second is a practical correction addressed to the people who need accurate information. The third records a small change that would reduce the chance of repeating the conduct. Those drafts may be brief, but they should each perform their own task. Ask a wise person for help where the repair involves a formal process or sensitive information.
Prayer. Father, I bring my sin into Your light. Forgive me, renew my heart, and give me courage to tell the truth and make the repair that belongs to me. Amen.
Chapter 7 As We Forgive Our Debtors
Listen without rehearsing a counterattack. Forgiveness can begin while trust still needs patient rebuilding.
Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee? — Matthew 18:33, KJV

Read Matthew 18:21–35. Peter asks about the limit of forgiveness. Jesus tells of a servant who receives mercy for an enormous debt and then refuses mercy over a much smaller one. The king’s question identifies the connection. Having received mercy changes what the servant owes in compassion toward another person.

Forgiveness may start with prayer long before trust can be rebuilt. A person can refuse revenge and still tell the truth about harm. Reconciliation involves more than one person. Decisions about safety, restitution, and renewed access may require evidence and wise counsel. The Lord’s Prayer can lead you to bring your resentment to the Father while still taking responsibility for protecting people who could be harmed.
Scriptural testimony · Joseph names the wrong
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. — Genesis 50:20, KJV

Joseph’s brothers feared retaliation after their father died. Joseph named their intention as evil and spoke of what God brought about. A reader can learn from both parts of his sentence. Describe the wrong truthfully, then ask God how you can refuse to repay harm with harm. Joseph’s conduct in Genesis 50 includes reassurance and provision. Your faithful response may look different where circumstances and safety differ.

Practice. Name the offense in one sentence. Identify one form of retaliation you are tempted to pursue. Pray about surrendering it. Record a boundary or accountability step that remains necessary, and ask a trustworthy person to help you keep it.
Pray while the debt still feels large
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you. — Ephesians 4:32, KJV

Read Ephesians 4:25–32 as a whole. Paul places forgiveness beside truthfulness, anger, useful work, and speech that builds up. The setting is a community in which people have to live with one another’s words and actions. A tenderhearted response can begin by giving up the next harmful message you were preparing to send. You can then ask what truth needs to be spoken, who should hear it, and what help would make the conversation responsible.

The phrase “even as” points the reader toward the forgiveness received through Christ. Remember a particular wrong you confessed and the mercy on which you relied. Then bring the present offense to God in words that acknowledge its weight. Ask for grace at the point where resentment is shaping your conduct. This prayer may need to be repeated when the incident returns to mind. Record what the prayer leads you to do differently, especially in the way you speak about the person.
Scriptural testimony · Stephen prays while suffering
And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. — Acts 7:60, KJV

Read Acts 7:54–60. Stephen’s final prayer comes amid violent wrongdoing. The account names the people’s actions and records the witness of Stephen’s prayer. A reader should allow both the harm and the prayer to remain visible. The story gives language for entrusting judgment to God and asking mercy for people who have done wrong. It also shows why Christian teaching about forgiveness must take the suffering of the person harmed seriously.
Visual summary
Release personal revenge
Keep wise boundaries
Rebuild trust through evidence
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Practice the next faithful response

Imagine a fictional member of a family in Kumasi who learns that a relative shared private information. The person can pray for help to refuse retaliation and then explain which information must remain private in future. If the relative ignores that boundary, reducing what is shared may be wise. Write a sentence of prayer and a sentence about the boundary. Ask whether each sentence performs its task clearly and whether either places pressure on the injured person to conceal the harm.
Prayer. Father, remember me in Your mercy. Help me speak truthfully about the harm I have received and surrender revenge. Give me wisdom about the next step. Amen.
Chapter 8 Lead Us Not into Temptation
Change the setting before temptation grows. A practical boundary can support the prayer you have just prayed.
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. — Matthew 26:41, KJV

In Gethsemane, Jesus gives the disciples two verbs. They are to watch and pray. Prayer can be joined to attention. Notice the conditions in which you are quick to give in. A person who replies harshly when exhausted can decide in daylight what to do when a provocative message arrives at night. That preparation gives the request a place to work in ordinary life.
Scriptural testimony · Peter’s confidence meets pressure

Read Matthew 26:31–35, 69–75. Peter confidently says he will remain faithful. Later, questioned in the courtyard, he denies knowing Jesus. Compare the circumstances of the promise with the circumstances of the denial. A promise made among friends can feel easy to keep. The danger becomes clearer when someone asks the same person to speak in front of a hostile crowd.
Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man: — James 1:13, KJV

James prevents a mistaken reading of the Lord’s Prayer. God does not entice people to evil. Asking the Father to keep you from entering temptation is an admission of need and a request for His guidance. It can lead you to arrange help before an old pattern returns. If you know a conversation is likely to stir resentment, choose a time, a setting, and a person who can help you respond wisely.
Practice. Identify a warning sign, one action you can take at that sign, and a person you can ask to support you. Write the first words you will use. Pray over the plan before the situation comes.
Watch where the opportunity begins

But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death. — James 1:14–15, KJV

James describes a movement. A desire draws the person, enticement makes a choice attractive, and the chosen course bears consequences. If you only examine the final act, you may miss the earlier point where a faithful response was available. Someone who regularly loses their temper in a family discussion might notice that they begin rehearsing accusations before the conversation starts. Bringing that rehearsal to God can help them prepare a truthful question instead.

Read James 1:12–18. The surrounding verses speak of endurance, God’s generosity, and His word of truth. Keep those resources in view while studying temptation. A believer can name the desire honestly and ask for help before it turns into a plan. Tell a trustworthy person what support would help, and arrange an action specific enough to use at the warning sign.
Scriptural testimony · Joseph leaves the room
And he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out. — Genesis 39:12, KJV, final sentence

Read Genesis 39:7–20. Joseph has already refused the repeated invitations and explained his responsibility toward his master and toward God. At the moment when the situation becomes immediate, he leaves. The story then records a false accusation and a painful consequence. Faithfulness in the scene has a cost. Read the whole account so that the decision to leave remains meaningful even though the outcome was difficult.

A practical response to temptation may require leaving a place, ending a private exchange, or asking someone else to take over a task. Decide the action beforehand where possible. If you are tempted to alter an account to hide an error, choose to show the original figures to the person responsible for reviewing them. The earlier the question is brought into the light, the more room there is to respond responsibly.
Visual summary
Recognize the pressure
Ask for help and change access
Choose the way of escape
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Workbook rehearsal

Write the first sentence you will say when you notice your warning sign. Practice it aloud. It might be “I need time to check the record before I answer” or “I’m going to step away and come back when I can speak calmly.” Pray over the sentence and identify what could prevent you from using it. Arrange the support you need before the situation returns.
Prayer. Father, guide me away from the paths where I readily stumble. Help me notice the danger early, ask for help, and choose what honors You. Amen.
Chapter 9 Deliver Us from Evil
Let trusted believers stand beside you. Ask for help with a concrete need and a wise next step.
And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen. — Matthew 6:13, KJV

Deliverance asks for active help from God. The closing words return the attention to His kingdom, power, and glory. When a threat occupies your thoughts, the pattern of the prayer lets you name the danger while remembering whose power you are asking for. That can make room for a wise action alongside faith. Where someone is in danger, seek appropriate protection and help while you pray.
Scriptural testimony · The church prays for Peter
Peter therefore was kept in prison: but prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him. — Acts 12:5, KJV

Acts 12:1–17 records both James’s death and Peter’s deliverance. The church prays for Peter during a crisis that has already caused real loss. Read what happens when Peter reaches the house where people are praying. Rhoda recognizes his voice. The people are surprised. Luke records their bewilderment as part of the story. Their prayer matters without requiring them to know exactly how events will unfold.

Think of a person under pressure now. Ask for a specific protection. You may be able to check whether they are safe, stay with them while they seek help, or contact someone who has responsibility for the situation. Respect their privacy and act appropriately where safeguarding obligations apply. A practical step should fit the danger the person actually faces.

Practice. Write the threat, the protection you are asking for, and one wise action within your reach. Ask someone trustworthy to pray with you where appropriate. Revisit the request after you have better information.
Ask for deliverance with your attention on God
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. — Psalm 46:1, KJV

Read Psalm 46 in full. The opening claim is followed by images of upheaval. Trouble is present in the song, and God is named as refuge within it. Later the psalm directs the hearer to behold God’s works and acknowledge His rule. The pattern gives you a way to pray when alarming information keeps repeating in your thoughts. Name the danger, read the claim about God, and ask what help and action are needed now.

Some circumstances require immediate protective action. Call the appropriate local help when someone is in danger, find a safe place, and involve responsible people while you pray. Where the concern is uncertain, gather reliable information before circulating an accusation. A prayer for protection can include a request for discernment about what is happening and whom to contact.
Scriptural testimony · Jehoshaphat brings the threat before God
O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. — 2 Chronicles 20:12, KJV

Read 2 Chronicles 20:1–22. Jehoshaphat receives news of an approaching force, seeks the Lord, and calls the people together. His prayer recalls God’s rule and brings the present danger into that account. The verse includes a direct admission that they do not know what to do. Such words can help someone pray honestly when they feel expected to sound certain.

The response in the chapter includes a particular instruction for this particular crisis. Read it carefully before making an application. Your own next step will need to fit your circumstances and responsibilities. Ask which facts you know, which people need protection, and which person has authority to act. A clear account of those matters can help you seek counsel and avoid a rushed decision.
Visual summary
Bring the danger to God
Accept wise support
Take a responsible action
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Carry the prayer into a group

If a congregation is praying for a threatened family, agree which details may be shared. Let the family state what support would help where possible. Assign a responsible person to coordinate practical offers so the family does not have to answer repeated calls. In the prayer meeting, name the protection sought and ask for wisdom for those providing help. Follow up on any commitment and update the prayer using confirmed information.
Prayer. Father, deliver us from evil. Protect those who are in danger and show me how to act wisely. Yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory. Amen.
Chapter 10 A Week of Praying Scripture
A weekly rhythm gives Scripture room to shape the requests, choices, and relationships of ordinary life.
Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving; — Colossians 4:2, KJV

Colossians joins perseverance, watchfulness, and gratitude. Watchfulness gives the week a way to learn. Write down what you ask and notice what actually changes. Thanksgiving helps you see provision that could be missed while waiting for another request. Use your notebook to name both unresolved needs and reasons to give thanks.
1. Come to the Father. Read Matthew 6:6–9 and Hebrews 4:16. Name the need that has been hardest to admit and ask for mercy or grace in plain words.
2. Honor His name. Read Psalm 103:8–14. Name one attribute of God and one interaction in which you can honor Him.
3. Pray for His kingdom. Read Matthew 9:35–38. Ask for workers in a particular place. Learn one thing from someone who serves there.
4. Submit a decision. Read Matthew 26:39 and Romans 12:2. Write what you desire, one responsibility, and one fact to check.
5. Ask for daily bread. Read Matthew 6:11 and Exodus 16:4. Name a present need for your household and for another person.
6. Confess and forgive. Read Matthew 6:12 and Psalm 51:10. Tell God what you did. Identify an appropriate repair and pray about the resentment you want to release.
7. Watch and seek protection. Read Matthew 6:13 and 26:41. Name an early warning sign and a faithful response you can prepare.

At the end of the week, reread your notes. Identify one request that became more accurate as you learned more. Give thanks for any help you recognized. Choose one concern to carry into next week and one action you can take because you prayed about it. ### Keep a record that helps you pray again
I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old. — Psalm 77:11, KJV

Read Psalm 77:1–15. The psalm begins with distress and difficult questions. The speaker then turns to remembering and meditating on God’s works. The movement can teach you how to use a prayer record. An entry can hold a question honestly while also recording a reason to remember God’s faithfulness. When you reread the week, identify both the unresolved matter and the help you received.

Use four short fields in your notebook: the passage read, the request made, the action taken, and what you learned. If a request changes because you discover new information, preserve the original wording and add a dated correction. You can then see how listening and learning made the prayer more accurate. Keep another person’s sensitive details private and record only what serves your own faithful follow-through.
Scriptural testimony · Daniel keeps his appointment

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime. — Daniel 6:10, KJV

Read Daniel 6:1–23. Daniel’s practice preceded the prohibition. The phrase “as he did aforetime” shows that the crisis meets an established habit of prayer and thanksgiving. That can guide a person building a routine. Choose a time you can realistically keep. Prepare a place for the passage and your notebook. Begin with a short period you can give attentively and allow the practice to grow through use.
Visual summary
Read Scripture carefully
Pray one clear response
Review the day with honesty
Apply one step to a situation you face today.
Review with a companion

At the end of the week, choose one prayer you are comfortable sharing with a trusted believer. Explain which verse guided it and what you learned. Ask the person to read the passage with you. They may notice a context or an application you missed. Receive that as an opportunity to make the next prayer more faithful to Scripture.

Then decide which practice to carry into the next week. You might keep the same time, pray for one person each day, or return to one petition of the Lord’s Prayer. Record a definite date for reviewing the practice. A small commitment you can keep gives you a place to begin again when a busy day disrupts the routine.
